name: Shared craft science
summary: Shared scientific mechanisms and materials of Indian hand-block printing: metal-mordant complexation of anthraquinone reds, iron-tannin blacks and their fibre damage, indigo vat reduction and re-oxidation, physical resists, tannin pre-treatment, cloth preparation, sun bleaching and print-paste rheology. Mechanisms are stated only as far as the cited literature supports. Several rest on studies of other systems (Turkey red, paper, modern screen printing, pure clay films) and are flagged as analogies.

sources.title: Fiber-Safe Extraction of Red Mordant Dyes from Hair Fibers
sources.author: Erica J. Tiedemann; Yiqi Yang
sources.publisher: Journal of the American Institute for Conservation 34(3):195-206
sources.notes: Peer-reviewed conservation chemistry. Mordants as metal salts forming insoluble dye complexes; figure of a Ca-Al alizarin lake adapted from Kiel & Heertjes; alizarin forms six-member chelate rings with Al; acid extraction 'probably' works by replacing the metal ion with H+; large complexes likely physically trapped. Study is on hair (protein) fibres; mechanism statements are general.

sources.title: Turkey red dyeing in late-19th century Glasgow: Interpreting the historical process through re-creation and chemical analysis for heritage research and conservation (PhD thesis)
sources.author: Julie Hodges Wertz
sources.notes: Alum = potassium aluminium sulfate; aluminium acetate ('red liquor') considered better for cellulose; red colour is a lake of alizarin, aluminium and calcium; 27Al ssNMR shows six-fold coordinated Al on oiled-and-alumed calico and replica Turkey red; tannins chelate metals and 'probably' attract more aluminium. Context is European Turkey red (oil-mordant process), not Indian block printing.

sources.title: Experimental Treatment for Black-dyed Cotton Textiles Using Japanese Adhesives Funori and Nikawa
sources.author: Ajla Redzic; Moe Sato; Yae Ichimiya; Hisae Watanabe; Noriko Hayakawa
sources.publisher: Science for Conservation (Hozon Kagaku) No. 63, Tokyo National Research Institute for Cultural Properties
sources.notes: Lab study (ferrous sulfate + tannic acid on cotton). Introduction (citing earlier literature): iron + tannins give blacks/greys/browns; acidic process causing hydrolytic degradation of cellulose; iron-catalysed decomposition makes fibre weak and brittle; analogous to iron-gall-ink corrosion. Own measurement: extract pH of unaged dyed control 4.08 vs 6.85 undyed; pH falls and fragility rises with accelerated ageing. No aged undyed tensile control, so the strength loss is not isolated to iron in this study.

sources.title: Microbial Communities Associated With Indigo Fermentation That Thrive in Anaerobic Alkaline Environments
sources.author: Keiichi Aino; Kikue Hirota; Takahiro Okamoto; Zhihao Tu; Hidetoshi Matsuyama; Isao Yumoto
sources.notes: Indigo insoluble, leucoindigo soluble; reduction by indigo-reducing bacteria or sodium dithionite; brief air exposure oxidises leucoindigo; traditional vats kept at pH > 10.3-10.5 with lime hydrate; anaerobic alkaline conditions. Japanese sukumo vats.

sources.title: Influence of Cotton Pre-Treatment on Dyeing with Onion and Pomegranate Peel Extracts
sources.author: Lea Botteri; Anja Miljković; Martinia Ira Glogar
sources.notes: Cotton impurities (pectin, proteins, organic acids, waxes, fats) give hydrophobicity; scouring removes them; most natural dyes have affinity for protein rather than cellulose fibres; mordants key for fastness; iron salts gave the most achromatic shades; pomegranate peel (28% tannins) is a tannin dye and the authors attribute part of its behaviour to tannin acting as a mordant (interpretation, not measured).

sources.title: Enzymatic desizing of cotton: a review
sources.author: Kiro Mojsov
sources.publisher: International Journal of Management, IT and Engineering 4(1)
sources.notes: Warp threads coated with sizing agent (mostly starch) to prevent breakage; size must be removed before dyeing; amylase desizing. Review in a lower-tier journal; industrial context.

sources.title: The influence of mixed thickeners on printing over lyocell knitted fabric
sources.author: Nahida Akter; Nasrin Akter; Mahfuza Pervin; Md. Reazuddin Repon
sources.notes: Print sharpness, penetration and colour yield depend on paste viscosity and rheology; viscosity depends on the thickener; low-viscosity paste spreads and penetrates deeply; pseudoplastic paste has lower viscosity as shear rate increases; guar gum (galactomannan) pastes above 0.5% are pseudoplastic. Modern reactive-dye screen printing on lyocell: used here only as an analogue for block-printing pastes.

sources.title: Bleaching cotton in textile conservation: a closer look using atomic force microscopy
sources.author: Rana T. A. Salem; Karen Thompson; Mahesh Uttamlal
sources.notes: Photochemical and chemical attack can yellow cotton; discolouration lessened by oxidative or reductive bleaching; bleaching generally accepted to impart damage. Does not study sunlight bleaching itself.

sources.title: Comprehensive Review on Fruit of Terminalia chebula: Traditional Uses, Phytochemistry, Pharmacology, Toxicity, and Pharmacokinetics
sources.author: Changjian Wang et al.
sources.notes: Fruit tannins predominantly hydrolysable (gallotannins, ellagitannins, chebulic ellagitannins incl. chebulagic/chebulinic acid); 60 tannin compounds reported; during sunlight-drying of the fruit these degrade to gallic, ellagic and chebulic acids. No dyeing content.

sources.title: Indian Block-Printed Textiles: Past and Present
sources.author: Yael Rosenfield
sources.notes: Met Perspectives article dated 15 Nov 2016 (author role not stated on page). Cleaning with camel dung, castor oil, soda ash, sun bleaching 'by oxidation'; myrobalan (harde) as mordant precursor; alum paste fixes red only where printed; on the 13th-14th c. Met fragment the darker purple was printed with iron acetate from fermented scrap iron which with myrobalan caused fibre loss; Dabu mud resist with crack lines; indigo oxidises on air exposure; Indian red dye plants (Al, munjeet, chay); synthetic alizarin and indigo common today.

sources.title: Chintz (process sample), museum no. T.1-1920
sources.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
sources.notes: Coromandel Coast process: alum and iron mordants applied by kalam; chay-root bath gives red on alum and black on iron; wax resist for indigo; cloth washed and bleached between colours. Year is acquisition (made c.1919).

sources.title: Charting Chintz: Making the Fabric
sources.author: Alka Raman
sources.notes: Experimental reconstruction (Beaulieu manuscript): scouring, myrobalan and milk soaks, alum (red) and iron-water (black) outlines, madder bath under 60 C, repeated dunging and sun bleaching (sun lamps substituted). Year approximate (page shows 2020-2026 copyright).

sources.title: Dyeing cotton fabrics is an ancient Indian art
sources.author: Amit Mitra
sources.notes: Science journalism (published 15 Dec 1992). For madder, cloth first dipped in tannic solution then mordanted; alum gives red, iron acetate black; in contemporary Masulipatnam iron acetate replaced indigo for large black areas despite its known corrosive qualities; indigo reduced by fermentation to soluble indigo white and fixed by air oxidation; resists of gum and mud or wax.

sources.title: Block printing the impermeable clay Dabu
sources.author: Craft Revival Trust
sources.publisher: Google Arts & Culture (Craft Revival Trust archive)
sources.notes: Archive caption (Craft Revival Trust, 2009, Deesa, Gujarat): Dabu paste of dried river-bed silt, local natural gum, lime, sugar-cane molasses and water, kneaded several days and strained; sawdust sprinkled; sun-dried till hard; dip-dyed; repeated per colour. Documentation of one workshop, not chemical analysis.

sources.title: Effects of Aqueous Light Bleaching on the Subsequent Aging of Paper
sources.author: Terry Trosper Schaeffer; Mary T. Baker; Victoria Blyth-Hill; Dianne van der Reyden
sources.publisher: Journal of the American Institute for Conservation 31(3):289-311
sources.notes: Peer-reviewed conservation science on light bleaching of wet (immersed) paper, by sunlight or lamps. Mechanism statement: a chromophore absorbs light and is converted to a reactive peroxide or free radical, which causes (usually oxidative) change; chromophores become colourless products; light can also degrade paper components. Paper, not cotton cloth: analogue only for Indian sun bleaching.

sources.title: Production and validation of model iron-tannate dyed textiles for use as historic textile substitutes in stabilisation treatment studies
sources.author: Helen Wilson; Chris Carr; Marei Hacke
sources.notes: Peer-reviewed, with undyed controls. Fe(II) + hydrolysable tannins form blue-black iron(III)-tannate, colour from Fe(III)-O charge transfer; cellulose can bind tannic acid (H-bonding) and metal ions; dyed textiles surface pH 2.65-3.91 vs 5.36-7.46 undyed; dyed cotton lost tensile strength faster and more than undyed during accelerated ageing (80 C, 58% RH), attributed to acid hydrolysis and metal-catalysed oxidation. Model dyes from iron salt + tannic acid, not Indian iron acetate/myrobalan.

sources.title: Topology of desiccation crack patterns in clay and invariance of crack interface area with thickness
sources.author: Tajkera Khatun; Tapati Dutta; Sujata Tarafdar
sources.publisher: arXiv:1412.2842 (preprint); published in The European Physical Journal E (2015), doi:10.1140/epje/i2015-15083-6
sources.notes: Fetched the arXiv preprint (published version not read). Drying clay (bentonite) slurry films on glass: below a critical cracking thickness films dry without cracking; crack spacing is of the order of film thickness; thicker layers give fewer, wider cracks; composition, drying rate, humidity, substrate affect patterns. Pure clay on glass, not Dabu on cloth: physical analogue only.

concepts.title: Aluminium (alum) mordant complexation
concepts.summary: Mordants are metal salts that form an insoluble complex with dye molecules.
concepts.body_md:
Mordants are metal salts that form an insoluble complex with dye molecules. [S1]

In Indian block printing, a paste of the mordant alum fixes the red dye to the cotton only where the paste was applied. [S10]

27Al solid-state NMR of oiled-and-alumed calico and replica Turkey red indicates aluminium in a six-fold coordination complex with oxygen; aluminium not in the lake likely remains as carboxylates. [S2]

In the Turkey red process, the purpose of the alum or aluminium acetate bath is to imbue the oiled cotton with aluminium ions, the basis of the colour complex formed in dyeing. [S2]

Mordants were found to be of key importance for the fastness of natural dyes on cotton. [S5]

Solid-state NMR (ssNMR), a variation in which the analyte is not solvated, was used here for in situ analysis of oiled calico.

concepts.title: Alizarin (madder) metal-lake formation
concepts.summary: The red colour complex is a lake of alizarin, aluminium and calcium; other hydroxy-anthraquinone dyes also complex.
concepts.body_md:
The red colour complex is a lake of alizarin, aluminium and calcium; other hydroxy-anthraquinone dyes also complex. [S2]

Alizarin molecules can form six-member chelate rings with aluminium ions; large complexes may be partly physically trapped within the fibre. [S1]

Strong-acid extraction probably releases the dye by replacing the metal ion with hydrogen ions. [S1]

In Coromandel chintz, chay root reacts with alum mordant to give red and with iron mordant to give black. [S11]

Alum gives red when used with madder; iron acetate gives black. [S13]

On a 13th-14th-century Indian block-printed fragment at the Met, the darker purple area had been printed with iron acetate before the red dye bath. [S10]

Indian red dyes (Morinda citrifolia/Al, Rubia cordifolia/munjeet, chay root) are chemically different from dyer's madder; most artisans now use synthetic alizarin. [S10]

claims.text: The red colour complex is a lake of alizarin, aluminium and calcium; other hydroxy-anthraquinone dyes also complex.

evidence.quote: 3.8.1 Lake complex It has long been known that the complex that creates the brilliant red colour in Turkey red is a lake of alizarin, aluminium, and calcium,264 though a more comprehensive definition includes the other hydroxyanthraquinone dyes that complex as well.

claims.text: Alizarin molecules can form six-member chelate rings with aluminium ions; large complexes may be partly physically trapped within the fibre.
claims.quote: The alizarin molecules are capable of forming six-member chelate rings with aluminum ions.

evidence.quote: The alizarin molecules are capable of forming six-member chelate rings with aluminum ions.
It is also likely that the large complexes are physically trapped within the fiber.

claims.text: Strong-acid extraction probably releases the dye by replacing the metal ion with hydrogen ions.

evidence.quote: The chemical structures of alizarin (a) and the calcium-aluminum lake of alizarin (b) (adapted from Kiel and Heertjes 1963a ) The conventional extraction method, using strong acid, probably functions by replacing hydrogen ions for the metal ion, thus releasing the metal ion from the complex.

claims.text: In Coromandel chintz, chay root reacts with alum mordant to give red and with iron mordant to give black.

evidence.quote: The cotton is then submerged in a dye bath of chay root, a natural red dye from the Coromandel Coast. The chay reacts with the alum mordant to produce red, and with the iron mordant to produce black.

claims.text: Alum gives red when used with madder; iron acetate gives black.

evidence.locator: § "Dyeing cotton fabrics is an ancient Indian art"
evidence.quote: Iron acetate would result in a black colour and alum would make it red. Black was used only to outline patterns whereas for larger areas a combination of indigo and madder, or deep indigo, was preferred.

claims.text: On a 13th-14th-century Indian block-printed fragment at the Met, the darker purple area had been printed with iron acetate before the red dye bath.

evidence.quote: The darker shade of purple at the center of the leaves was block printed with a paste of iron acetate made of fermented scrap iron, which together with the myrobalan tannin created the corrosive dye that caused fiber loss.
Fragment (front [left], reverse [right]), 13th-14th century.

claims.text: Indian red dyes (Morinda citrifolia/Al, Rubia cordifolia/munjeet, chay root) are chemically different from dyer's madder; most artisans now use synthetic alizarin.

evidence.quote: These plants include some of the following varieties: Indian mulberry ( Morinda citrifolia L. ), also known as Al; Indian madder or munjeet ( Rubia cordifolia ); and chay root ( Oldenlandia umbellata L. ).
In India today, most artisans often use synthetic alizarin-an orange or red crystalline compound-though a discerning customer sometimes requests both Al and munjeet.

concepts.title: Iron-tannin black and iron-catalysed fibre degradation
concepts.summary: Iron mordant and tannins have long been combined to achieve deep blacks, greys and browns.
concepts.body_md:
Iron mordant and tannins have long been combined to achieve deep blacks, greys and browns. [S3]

Iron-mordant dyeing with tannins is an acidic process causing hydrolytic degradation of cellulose; the iron-catalysed reaction makes the fibre weak and brittle. [S3]

Iron-tannate-dyed cotton had an extract pH of 4.08 against 6.85 for undyed cotton; pH decreased with accelerated ageing and the longest-aged samples were extremely fragile. [S3]

On a Met Indian block-printed fragment, iron acetate made from fermented scrap iron, together with myrobalan tannin, formed a corrosive dye that caused fibre loss. [S10]

In contemporary Masulipatnam kalamkari, iron acetate is used for black outlines and has replaced indigo for large black areas, despite its known corrosive qualities. [S13]

Among aluminium, copper and iron mordants on cotton, iron gave the most achromatic (dull, dark) shades. [S5]

Ferrous ions with hydrolysable tannins form blue-black iron(III)-tannate complexes; the colour is due to reversible charge transfer across the Fe(III)-O bond. [S16]

Model iron-tannate-dyed cotton was acidic (surface pH 2.65-3.91 vs 5.36-7.46 undyed) and lost tensile strength faster and more than undyed controls in accelerated ageing. [S16]

The degradation is attributed to acid hydrolysis and metal-catalysed oxidation. [S16]

claims.text: Iron mordant and tannins have long been combined to achieve deep blacks, greys and browns.

evidence.quote: Iron mordant and tannins, combined to achieve dark colours (deep blacks, greys, and browns), have a long history together.

claims.text: Iron-mordant dyeing with tannins is an acidic process causing hydrolytic degradation of cellulose; the iron-catalysed reaction makes the fibre weak and brittle.
claims.quote: the iron-catalyst reaction decomposes the fibre, making it weak and brittle

evidence.quote: Dyeing with iron-mordant (ferrous() sulfate) in combination with tannins, dyes derived from plants and trees, naturally containing acids such as gallic acid, tannic acid, ellagic acid, represents an acidic process that causes hydrolytic degradation of protein in animal fibres, and cellulose in vegetable fibres.
When environmental conditions are met, the iron-catalyst reaction decomposes the fibre, making it weak and brittle3)5).

claims.text: Iron-tannate-dyed cotton had an extract pH of 4.08 against 6.85 for undyed cotton; pH decreased with accelerated ageing and the longest-aged samples were extremely fragile.

evidence.quote: Furthermore, results suggest that nikawa consolidation treatment has the potential to restore the tensile strength of iron-tannate dyed highly deteriorated cotton textile samples, exhibited in samples with accelerated ageing of 3 days before and after the treatment.

In samples aged for 3 days, funori was still effective, more so than nikawa, while in the most fragile samples artificially aged for the longest period, 3 days before and after the treatment, detection yielded only sample with nikawa consolidation.

claims.text: On a Met Indian block-printed fragment, iron acetate made from fermented scrap iron, together with myrobalan tannin, formed a corrosive dye that caused fibre loss.

evidence.quote: The darker shade of purple at the center of the leaves was block printed with a paste of iron acetate made of fermented scrap iron, which together with the myrobalan tannin created the corrosive dye that caused fiber loss.

The two Indian block prints at The Met are part of a group of early Islamic textiles, also known as the Fustat (Fostat) group, Indo-Egyptian, and Egypto-Arabic textiles, depending on the prevailing understanding of their provenance.

claims.text: In contemporary Masulipatnam kalamkari, iron acetate is used for black outlines and has replaced indigo for large black areas, despite its known corrosive qualities.

evidence.locator: § "Dyeing cotton fabrics is an ancient Indian art"
evidence.quote: Alizarin has replaced seravar and chay earlier used for madder. The mordant for outlining in black remains unchanged, but iron acetate has replaced indigo for dyeing larger areas black, despite its known corrosive qualities.

evidence.locator: § "Dyeing cotton fabrics is an ancient Indian art"
evidence.quote: Contemporary kalamkari techniques show various departures from the past. In Masulipatnam, mordant is uniformly printed with a block.

claims.text: Among aluminium, copper and iron mordants on cotton, iron gave the most achromatic (dull, dark) shades.

evidence.quote: The sample pre-treated with ferrum salts, as it was expected, achieved the most achromatic shade with the lowest chroma C* = 23.56.
By processing pre-treated yarns with metal salts of copper, aluminium and ferrum (mordants) the whiteness and yellowness index also change.

claims.text: Ferrous ions with hydrolysable tannins form blue-black iron(III)-tannate complexes; the colour is due to reversible charge transfer across the Fe(III)-O bond.

evidence.quote: On combination with ferrous ions hydrolysable tannins form blue-black coloured iron(III)-tannate dye complexes; the colour being due to a reversible charge transfer across the Fe(III)-O bond in the iron(III)-tannate, or iron(III)-gallate, complex [ 2 ].

evidence.quote: As seen with historic iron-tannate dyed objects, the dyed cotton, abaca, and silk textiles lost tensile strength faster and more significantly than undyed equivalents during accelerated thermal ageing and all of the dyed model textiles, most notably the cotton, discoloured more than the undyed equivalents

claims.text: The degradation is attributed to acid hydrolysis and metal-catalysed oxidation.

evidence.quote: the dyed textiles correlates well with their initial surface pH (Table 3 ), iron content (Table 2 ), and the presence of iron in the structurally important internal areas of the dyed fibres, suggesting that the degradation has occurred by acid hydrolysis and metal-catalysed oxidation,

concepts.title: Indigo vat reduction and air re-oxidation
concepts.summary: Indigo is not soluble in water whereas leucoindigo is; indigo is transformed to leucoindigo by indigo-reducing bacteria.
concepts.body_md:
Indigo is not soluble in water whereas leucoindigo is; indigo is transformed to leucoindigo by indigo-reducing bacteria. [S4]

Fermentation reduction has in many operations been replaced by chemical reduction with sodium dithionite. [S4]

Traditional indigo fermentation is kept under anaerobic, high-pH conditions, above pH 10.3-10.5 using lime hydrate. [S4]

Dyed textiles are briefly exposed to air to oxidise leucoindigo back to indigo. [S4]

In Indian resist-dyed cloth, the dye oxidises to the insoluble blue form on exposure to air, adhering to the fibres. [S10]

Indigo is reduced to soluble 'indigo white' for dyeing and fixed to the fibre by air oxidation. [S13]

claims.text: Indigo is not soluble in water whereas leucoindigo is; indigo is transformed to leucoindigo by indigo-reducing bacteria.
claims.quote: Although indigo is not soluble in water, leucoindigo is soluble in water.

evidence.quote: Indigo is transformed to leucoindigo by the action of indigo-reducing bacteria (indigo → leucoindigo) ( Figure 1 ). Although indigo is not soluble in water, leucoindigo is soluble in water.

claims.text: Fermentation reduction has in many operations been replaced by chemical reduction with sodium dithionite.

evidence.quote: Therefore, the fermentation procedure has been replaced with chemical reduction using sodium dithionite (Na 2 S 2 O 2 ).

claims.text: Traditional indigo fermentation is kept under anaerobic, high-pH conditions, above pH 10.3-10.5 using lime hydrate.

evidence.locator: § "Changes in the Microbiota in Aged Indigo Fermentation"
evidence.quote: Indigo fermentation occurs under anaerobic and high-pH conditions.

claims.text: Dyed textiles are briefly exposed to air to oxidise leucoindigo back to indigo.

evidence.quote: Therefore, leucoindigo penetrates textiles dipped in indigo fermentation fluid, followed by a brief exposure to air to oxidize leucoindigo (leucoindigo → indigo).

claims.text: In Indian resist-dyed cloth, the dye oxidises to the insoluble blue form on exposure to air, adhering to the fibres.

evidence.quote: Then, when the fabric is exposed to air, the dye oxidizes to the insoluble blue form, adhering to the fibers permanently.

My plan was to study and document current production methods of block-printed, tie-dyed, and painted textiles (also known as resist-dyed). The historic Indian block prints are ascribed to workshops of Gujarat, where a substantial printing tradition still exists.

claims.text: Indigo is reduced to soluble 'indigo white' for dyeing and fixed to the fibre by air oxidation.

evidence.locator: § "Dyeing cotton fabrics is an ancient Indian art"
evidence.quote: On oxidisation, indigo white is converted into granules of indigo blue which has then to be reduced through fermentation into soluble indigo white, before dyeing can begin.

evidence.locator: § "Dyeing cotton fabrics is an ancient Indian art"
evidence.quote: The fabric would first be dipped into a prepared dye vat and then exposed to air, so that the indigo white could revert into insoluble indigo blue and be bonded to the cotton fibre.

concepts.summary: The most common resist for indigo today is a mud paste called Dabu, which often shows characteristic crack lines where the dye penetrated cracks in the resist.

The most common resist for indigo today is a mud paste called Dabu, which often shows characteristic crack lines where the dye penetrated cracks in the resist. [S10]

A documented Dabu paste is made of river-bed silt, a local natural gum, lime, cane molasses and water, kneaded for several days, printed, covered with sawdust and sun-dried until hard before dip dyeing. [S14]

concepts.title: Tannin (myrobalan) pre-mordanting of cotton
concepts.summary: Tannins are polyphenolic compounds with many -OH groups that chelate metals; they were known to improve colour uptake by attracting more mordant and probably served as a secondary mordant attracting aluminium.
concepts.body_md:
Tannins are polyphenolic compounds with many -OH groups that chelate metals; they were known to improve colour uptake by attracting more mordant and probably served as a secondary mordant attracting aluminium. [S2]

Myrobalan (harde), a strong tannin from the fruit of the chebulic myrobalan, has traditionally been used as a mordant in India, applied as a precursor to dyeing. [S10]

For madder dyeing, cloth is first dipped in a tannic solution and mordants are then applied. [S13]

Most natural dyes have natural affinity for protein rather than cellulose fibres, which makes dyeing cotton problematic. [S5]

The authors attribute the behaviour of a tannin-rich extract (pomegranate peel, 28% tannins) on cotton partly to tannin behaving as a mordant. [S5]

Chintz reconstruction began with scouring, myrobalan soak and boil, and a myrobalan-and-milk soak before mordant outlining. [S12]
